s0.p1: **_Application Programming Interface_** (**API**) allows two systems to communicate with each other.
s0.p2: Suppose there is a set of services external to your application that greatly extend the functionality of your application.
s0.p3:
If there is some kind of API that provides you with access to these services, then this is an API.
That is, you do not need to include these services in your application, it does not matter to you what language they are written in, you only need to know how to activate them.
s0.p4:
Running on the client, your code constantly uses [**client-side web APIs**](⟦f6⟧)
(e.g., **⟦f0⟧**, **⟦f1⟧**, **⟦f2⟧**, **⟦f3⟧**, **⟦f4⟧**, **⟦f5⟧**).
s0.p6: You can connect to many web APIs remotely (e.g., [![ico-70 firebase]](⟦f8⟧) or [![ico-35 google-maps]](⟦f9⟧)).
s0.p7: As a rule, any application interacts with its backend API on the server.
s0.p8: A backend API provides an application with access to data stored on the server using **CRUD** methods.
s0.p9: **CRUD** (_create_, _read_, _update_, _delete_) are the four basic types of requests to the server.
s0.p10: To identify the type of request, an **access method**, or **verb**, is used to identify the operation on the resource.

s0.p18: Any API works on the principle of "request" — "response".
s0.p19: Your application sends a request, and if the request is valid, the API sends a response to the application.
s0.p20: The form of the request depends on the API.
s0.p21: This can be a method such as, **⟦f16⟧** or **⟦f17⟧**.
s0.p22: This can be an object whose properties and methods give you access to the capabilities of the browser API. All **⟦f18⟧** and **⟦f19⟧** objects are elements of the browser API.
s0.p23: This can be a constructor that you use to create objects that give you access to the capabilities of the browser API. For example, the **⟦f20⟧** constructor or the **⟦f21⟧**.
s0.p24: The main thing when interacting with the server API is to determine the concept “resource” and assign a unique identifier to each resource.
s0.p25: ^^For example, the resource can be information about the user. Then, knowing the unique identifier of the resource, you can send a request to the server API to obtain user data by its identifier (**GET**), you can send a request to change user data (**PUT** or **PATCH**) or send a request to create a new user (**POST**).^^
s0.p26: Thus, when interacting with a remote API, by the term “resource” we mean a **certain piece of information that has a unique identifier**.
s0.p27: ^^The difference between **URL** (Uniform Resource Locator) and **URI** (Uniform Resource Identifier) ​​is precisely that the **URL** specifies the exact location of the resource on the server, while the **URI** specifies only the resourceid. **URI** provides greater flexibility of the server API in terms of data placement and the form of its storage.^^
s0.p28: A resource can be a file stored on a server or a single record in a database.
s0.p29: For example, an image file may be stored on the server, but the same image may be stored in the database as a text string in the format of [**Base64**](⟦f22⟧).
s0.p30: Each API has documentation and specifications that define how information is transferred.
s0.p31: APIs can use HTTP requests to obtain information from a web application or web server.
s0.p32: In the case of a REST API, the request is made over the Internet, and takes the form of a certain web address called **⟦f23⟧** (access point to the remote API).
s0.p33: ^^The term "endpoint" is used not only in the context of REST APIs, but also in a broader sense in the field of information technology and networking.^^
s0.p34: ^^• In network protocols, endpoint can refer to any communication endpoint in a network, whether it is an IP address and port in TCP/IP, or an endpoint in message routing.^^
s0.p35: ^^• In SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) API endpoint also denotes the URL to which SOAP messages are sent. This is similar to the REST API, but is used in other protocols and data formats.^^
s0.p36: ^^• In the GraphQL API endpoint represents a single endpoint through which a client can request specific data using complex queries.^^
s0.p37: ^^• In microservices, an endpoint can denote any entry point for interacting with an individual microservice. Each microservice can have its own endpoints for different functionality.^^
s0.p38: ^^• More generally, an endpoint can refer to any point through which a resource or service is accessed, whether within a system or between different systems.^^

s0.p57: An endpoint in a REST API is the point that the client accesses to interact with the server.
s0.p58: It is not just a URL, but a combination of an API address and a route, which includes a resource identifier and information about what action to perform. It's like a web address, but with extra parts that specify what exactly needs to be done with the data.

s0.p69: APIs are typically classified as **SOAP** or **REST**, and both are used to access web services.
